h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Columbus, Georgia
intro:
Columbus is a river and mill city that became a military town, and its housing tells that story block by block. Mill houses climb the hills of Bibb City and North Highlands above the Chattahoochee. Craftsman bungalows and revival-style homes fill Midtown around Lakebottom Park. Brick ranches stretch south and east toward Fort Benning, where a steady flow of soldiers, families and civilian staff keeps rental demand alive year after year.

Genstone Construction helps investors, lenders and servicers price that range of housing before money is committed. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repair costs and checks your after-repair value. When you are ready, you receive a detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule, and a designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors in Columbus and across the river in Phenix City. We handle permits, historic review, inspections and lien waivers. No money changes hands before work begins, draws are matched to completed phases, and dumpsters are part of the number you see on day one.
housingStock:
Columbus was laid out in the 1820s on the falls of the Chattahoochee, and the river's water power built a textile economy that lasted well into the twentieth century. That heritage left several distinct layers of housing.

The Columbus Historic District, just south and east of downtown, contains some of the city's oldest homes: antebellum cottages, Greek Revival and Italianate houses, and late-Victorian homes, most of them frame construction on brick piers with tall ceilings, heart pine floors and original windows. Many have been restored; others still need significant structural and system work.

Mill neighborhoods grew up near the river. Bibb City, once a separate mill town before it merged with Columbus, and North Highlands and Rose Hill contain rows of small, closely spaced frame mill houses with simple gable roofs and front porches. They were built inexpensively, and many have shifting piers, original wiring and aging plumbing.

Midtown, including Wynnton, Dinglewood, Peacock Woods and the area around Lakebottom Park, developed in the early twentieth century with Craftsman bungalows, Tudor and Colonial revivals and some substantial homes on larger lots. These neighborhoods are among the most desirable in the city for buyers who want older homes.

After the Second World War, as Fort Benning expanded, Columbus spread south and east. Brick ranches from the 1950s through the 1970s fill neighborhoods such as Benning Hills and much of south and east Columbus. North Columbus filled in later with larger suburban homes.

The city sits on the Fall Line, so north Columbus has rolling Piedmont clay while areas to the south transition toward sandier soils. Hillside lots in the mill neighborhoods and older parts of Midtown often have tall rear crawlspaces or partial basements where drainage and settlement show up first. Termites, wood rot, lead paint and outdated wiring are recurring items across the older housing, while the mid-century ranches tend toward aging electrical panels, galvanized supply lines and cast-iron drains.

commonIssues.title: Mill house foundations and framing
commonIssues.body: Mill houses in Bibb City, North Highlands and Rose Hill were built quickly and economically, often on brick piers with minimal footings and light framing. After a century, many have settled unevenly, especially on sloping lots. Floors dip, walls rack and porches pull away. Releveling, adding piers on proper footings and replacing damaged sills and joists are typical first steps, and they need to be priced before any finish work is considered for these homes.

commonIssues.title: Outdated wiring and service
commonIssues.body: Older Columbus homes, including mill houses and Historic District properties, may still contain knob-and-tube wiring or early cloth-insulated cable, along with small electrical services that cannot support modern appliances and air conditioning. Insurers often object, and buyers' inspectors flag it. In mid-century ranches, obsolete panel brands and undersized services also come up regularly. Electrical upgrades are frequently among the most important items in a Columbus rehab scope.

commonIssues.title: Termite damage and rot
commonIssues.body: West Georgia's warm, humid climate supports active termites year-round, and older wood-frame homes on low crawlspaces are especially vulnerable. Sills, rim joists, porch framing and window frames are the usual trouble spots. Rot from leaking roofs, clogged gutters and failed plumbing makes it worse. Every older Columbus house we scope gets a careful look underneath and around the base of the exterior walls before finishes are priced.

commonIssues.title: Base-area rental wear
commonIssues.body: Ranches near Fort Benning have often been rented to many households over the decades. Frequent moves, short-term owners and deferred maintenance leave a familiar pattern: worn flooring, patched drywall, aging HVAC systems, tired kitchens and baths, and small repairs done without permits. These homes rarely hide major structural surprises, but the accumulated wear adds up, and unpermitted changes such as enclosed carports or garages should be reviewed before they are counted as living space.

commonIssues.title: Drainage on hillside lots
commonIssues.body: Parts of Midtown and the mill neighborhoods sit on slopes where stormwater runs toward foundations. Heavy summer storms push water into crawlspaces and against basement walls, causing damp conditions, mold, rot and settlement. Gutters, downspout extensions, regrading and, where necessary, drainage systems are relatively inexpensive compared with the damage they prevent, and we put them near the top of the scope wherever we see evidence of water problems.

investorMarket:
Fort Benning shapes much of the Columbus investor market. Military households move on a regular cycle, and many prefer to rent rather than buy for a short assignment. That keeps steady demand for clean, functional single-family rentals in south and east Columbus, in neighborhoods such as Benning Hills, and across the river in Phenix City. Brick ranches there are the workhorses of many local rental portfolios.

Midtown is the main territory for retail flips. Buyers connected to Aflac, Global Payments, Synovus, the hospitals and Columbus State University look for renovated older homes in Wynnton, Dinglewood, Lakebottom and nearby streets. They expect quality kitchens and baths in houses that keep their original character.

North Columbus, with newer suburban homes, attracts families and buyers who want more space. Flips there compete with newer construction and must meet those expectations.

The mill neighborhoods offer some of the lowest purchase prices in the city. Bibb City has seen redevelopment interest, including the conversion of mill buildings along the river, and North Highlands and Rose Hill have a mix of rentals and owner-occupants. Renovation needs in these homes are often substantial, so careful scoping matters.

The Historic District offers restoration projects that can command strong prices but require patience, historic review and higher budgets.

Phenix City and Russell County, across the river in Alabama, operate under different permitting and licensing rules, so investors who buy on both sides of the Chattahoochee need scopes and budgets that reflect each jurisdiction.
permits:
Columbus and Muscogee County have operated as a consolidated government since 1971, so permits for most properties come through the Columbus Consolidated Government's inspections and code enforcement office. Properties in Harris County, Phenix City or Russell County use their own permitting offices, and work in Alabama follows that state's licensing rules.

Permits are generally required for structural repairs, foundation work, roof replacement involving decking or structure, electrical and plumbing alterations, HVAC replacement, additions and major exterior changes. Cosmetic work like painting and flooring usually does not need one. Electrical, plumbing and conditioned air permits must be pulled by trade contractors holding the matching Georgia license.

Columbus has local historic districts, including the downtown Historic District and others, where exterior changes go before the Board of Historic and Architectural Review. Window replacement, siding changes, porch alterations, new construction and demolition are typical items reviewed.

Inspections follow the usual rough-in and final sequence, and scheduling them efficiently matters on investor projects with carrying costs.

Our team checks historic designation, pulls permits, prepares review submissions, schedules inspections and collects lien waivers throughout the project, so you have a clean record for refinance or resale.
climate:
Columbus has long, hot and humid summers that put heavy demands on cooling systems. Properly sized HVAC, sealed ductwork, attic insulation and ventilation are standard parts of an investor scope here, because tenants and buyers notice immediately when a system struggles in July.

Humidity also feeds moisture problems in crawlspaces, bathrooms and closed-up vacant homes. Mold can develop quickly when air conditioning is off.

Severe thunderstorms are common in spring and summer, and the region occasionally sees tornado warnings. Roof work and open exterior walls are scheduled around forecasts and dried in quickly.

Winters are mild, though occasional hard freezes can damage exposed plumbing in vacant homes.

Spring and fall usually provide the most comfortable conditions for exterior painting, roofing and concrete work, and many investors time listings for spring, when military moves and buyer activity tend to increase.

faqs.q: Do you work in Phenix City as well as Columbus?
faqs.a: Yes. Many investors buy rentals on both sides of the Chattahoochee. Phenix City and Russell County are in Alabama, so permitting, licensing and inspection processes differ from those in Columbus. We coordinate licensed local contractors in each jurisdiction and note which office handles permits in your scope. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is available on either side of the river, which makes it easier to compare deals across the state line.

faqs.q: Are Bibb City and North Highlands mill houses worth renovating?
faqs.a: Some are, but only with a realistic budget. Mill houses are inexpensive to buy, yet many need foundation releveling, rewiring, plumbing replacement and termite repair before cosmetic work makes sense. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates those costs before you buy, so you can see whether expected rents or resale values leave enough margin for the full scope of work and your return on the project.

faqs.q: How does the Board of Historic and Architectural Review affect my project?
faqs.a: If the property sits in a local historic district, exterior changes such as replacing windows, altering porches, changing siding or adding square footage need review before permits issue. Interior work generally does not. We check designation before scoping, plan exterior work around what is likely to be approved, prepare the submission and keep interior work moving during review, which limits idle time on the project.

faqs.q: Do you work with out-of-state investors and service members?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Columbus rental owners live elsewhere, including service members who kept a house after a permanent change of station. A designated field manager posts photos at each milestone, each draw request is matched to finished work, and every trade signs a lien waiver. You can follow every stage and approve payments without traveling to Columbus, which is how most of our remote clients manage their properties.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Columbus, GA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Columbus, GA fix and flip renovations for Midtown bungalows and ranches near Fort Benning, scoped for VA buyers and priced before you make an offer.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Columbus, Georgia
fix-flip.intro:
Two very different flips dominate Columbus. One is the Midtown bungalow or revival-style house near Lakebottom Park, sold to a professional buyer who wants character and modern comfort in the same package. The other is the brick ranch in south or east Columbus, sold to a military family or first-time buyer using VA or FHA financing who needs a house that passes appraisal cleanly and does not drain their savings with repairs.

Genstone Construction scopes both. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and checks your ARV against renovated Columbus sales. If the numbers work, a detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule follows, often with more than one finish level priced side by side. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local contractors, handles permits and historic review, and documents progress so you can run the flip without living in Columbus.

sections.h2: Midtown Columbus flips: character plus comfort
sections.body:
Wynnton, Dinglewood, Peacock Woods, Weracoba and the streets around Lakebottom Park are where Columbus buyers pay for older homes with personality. Many of those buyers work for Aflac, Global Payments, Synovus, the hospitals or Columbus State University, and they compare your house with renovated neighbors and with newer homes in north Columbus.

Original features matter here. Heart pine or oak floors, plaster crown, mantels, built-ins and deep front porches add value when restored. At the same time, buyers expect open, well-equipped kitchens, primary bathrooms that feel current, enough closet space and fully modern electrical, plumbing and HVAC.

The tension is in the layout. Many Midtown homes have small, closed kitchens at the back of the house and a single bathroom. Opening the kitchen to an adjacent room and adding a second bath, sometimes by borrowing space from a back porch or oversized hall, often moves value more than any finish upgrade.

We price a mid-level and upgraded finish plan side by side when comps are uncertain, so you can make that call before demolition starts.

sections.h2: Ranch flips for VA buyers near Fort Benning
sections.body:
South and east Columbus ranches are bought largely by service members and military families, many of them using VA loans. That changes the scope in an important way: the house has to satisfy the appraiser's minimum property requirements as well as appeal to the buyer.

VA appraisers look for safe, sound and sanitary conditions. Peeling paint on pre-1978 homes, missing handrails, inoperable windows, roof leaks, exposed wiring, broken HVAC and evidence of termite damage can all lead to repair conditions that delay or derail a closing. We build those items into the original scope rather than waiting for the appraisal to find them.

Beyond the requirements, military buyers often have limited time to house hunt and want a home that is ready to move into. Clean, neutral finishes, updated kitchens and baths, durable flooring and reliable HVAC tend to win offers.

We also check for unpermitted garage or carport conversions, which are common in this stock. An appraiser may not count that space unless it was properly permitted and finished, which affects your ARV.

sections.h2: Keeping a Columbus flip schedule tight
sections.body:
Holding costs add up while a flip sits unfinished, and Columbus has a few particular schedule risks to plan around.

In the Historic District and other designated areas, exterior changes go before the Board of Historic and Architectural Review. We prepare those submissions early, scope exterior work to what is likely to be approved and keep interior demolition, framing and rough-ins moving while the review proceeds.

Older homes in Midtown and the mill neighborhoods can reveal hidden pier, framing or termite damage once floors are opened. Our scope includes a contingency for those findings so the job does not stop while a new budget is prepared.

Timing the listing also matters. Military moves tend to cluster in the warmer months, and many Columbus investors aim to have ranch flips ready when PCS season brings more buyers to town.

Our field manager schedules inspections so multiple trades are ready together and posts progress photos and milestones, which helps you coordinate photography, staging and your listing date with your agent.

faqs.q: Which Columbus neighborhoods are strongest for flips?
faqs.a: Midtown neighborhoods such as Wynnton, Dinglewood and the Lakebottom area tend to support renovations that preserve character, while south and east Columbus ranches often sell well to military and first-time buyers. North Columbus attracts buyers comparing against newer construction. Results vary by street, and our Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps you compare renovation costs against likely values before you commit. That is especially helpful when renovated sales on your street are few.

faqs.q: How do VA appraisals affect a Columbus flip?
faqs.a: VA appraisers check for safety, soundness and sanitary conditions. Items like peeling paint on older homes, roof leaks, missing handrails, inoperable windows or non-working HVAC can trigger repair requirements before closing. We include those items in the original scope, which reduces the chance of a delayed or renegotiated closing after you are already under contract with a military buyer. It also helps your buyer close on schedule before a report date.

faqs.q: Can you restore original features in a Midtown Columbus home?
faqs.a: Yes. Hardwood floors, plaster details, mantels, built-ins and front porches often add value with Midtown buyers. We will tell you which features are practical to restore and which cost more than they return. In historic districts, some exterior elements may need to remain for approval, and we plan the scope with that in mind from the beginning of the project.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Columbus, GA | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Columbus, GA BRRRR rehabs for brick ranches near Fort Benning and Midtown bungalows, built for the refinance and frequent military turnover.
brrrr.intro:
Few Georgia markets fit the BRRRR model as naturally as Columbus. Fort Benning supplies a constant stream of renters who need a house for a few years at a time, older ranches in south and east Columbus can often be bought below what renovated comps support, and Phenix City across the river adds another pool of similar inventory. The work is making sure the renovation supports the refinance appraisal and survives the frequent moves that come with military tenants.

Genstone Construction scopes Columbus BRRRR projects for both. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review tests the purchase against realistic repair costs and a defensible after-repair value. When it is time to refinance, Genstone Financial's DSCR rental loans are one option; you are free to bring your own lender. We coordinate licensed local contractors, handle permits and tie every draw to completed, documented work.

sections.h2: Columbus improvements that show up at refinance
sections.body:
Columbus appraisers tend to pull comps from a tight radius, and in the ranch neighborhoods around the base those comps are mostly updated brick homes with three bedrooms and one or two baths. The improvements that track most closely with value are an updated kitchen, renovated baths, new flooring, modern HVAC, a newer roof and a clean, well-kept exterior.

A second full bathroom is often the single most effective addition. Many ranches here were built with one bath, or with a bath and a half. Converting a half bath to a full bath, or carving one out of an oversized utility room, can bring a house in line with stronger comps.

Garage and carport conversions are common, but appraisers often discount them if they are unpermitted or poorly integrated. We scope conversions to code with permits through the consolidated government, so the space has documentation behind it.

The Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices these options so you can see which improvements support the appraisal you need and which mainly add cost.

sections.h2: Built for military move-ins and move-outs
sections.body:
Military tenants move often, and each move puts wear on floors, walls, doors and fixtures. A BRRRR property in Columbus has to absorb that without needing a full renovation every few years.

Luxury vinyl plank stands up to furniture and moving dollies better than carpet or laminate and handles humidity well. Scrubbable paint in a consistent color makes touch-ups quick. Solid-surface or quartz counters, sturdy cabinet hardware and simple, widely available fixtures keep turn costs down.

Door frames, door stops and corner protection may seem minor, but they prevent much of the damage moving crews cause.

Cooling reliability is essential in Columbus summers, and a failed air conditioner is often the first call a landlord gets. Properly sized equipment, sealed ducts, adequate attic insulation and clean condensate drainage reduce those calls.

Finally, water management, including gutters, grading and crawlspace vapor barriers, prevents the moisture problems that lead to rot and termite damage over a long hold.

sections.h2: Columbus areas where BRRRR tends to work
sections.body:
The brick ranch neighborhoods of south and east Columbus, including Benning Hills and the areas along Victory Drive and Buena Vista Road, are where many investors build BRRRR portfolios. Purchase prices there are often moderate, tenant demand from the base is steady, and the masonry stock reduces structural surprises.

Midtown bungalows can work if bought at the right price, but values there often make a retail flip more attractive than a hold.

Mill houses in Bibb City, North Highlands and Rose Hill are inexpensive, but foundation, wiring and termite issues can consume the equity you plan to pull out at refinance. Some investors find good deals there; others find the risk too high.

Phenix City offers similar ranch stock and rental demand on the Alabama side, with different permitting and licensing rules.

Which area suits your plan is your call, not ours; what we can do is lay out side by side what a ranch, a mill house and a Midtown bungalow would each cost to bring to a rentable, appraisable standard.

faqs.q: Can Genstone Financial refinance a Columbus BRRRR?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial is the lending arm of the Genstone Companies, and its DSCR rental loans are built for exactly this kind of cash-out step. You are under no obligation to use it. If you use it, coordinating documents such as the scope, permits, inspection sign-offs and completion photos can be simpler. We provide the same records to any lender you choose, so the appraiser and underwriter have what they need to evaluate the improvements.

faqs.q: Should I add a bathroom to a Columbus ranch rental?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many ranches near Fort Benning have a single full bath, and adding a second can improve both the appraisal and the rent. Whether it makes financial sense depends on the floor plan and plumbing layout. We price the addition in the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can compare its cost against the expected increase in value and rent before you commit.

faqs.q: How do you handle turns between military tenants?
faqs.a: Our Field Services group takes on the turn itself: cleaning, paint, small fixes and a walk-through inspection. We document conditions at move-out with photos to help with deposit decisions. If a turn reveals larger needs, such as a failing HVAC system or roof, our renovation team scopes and prices the work so you can decide quickly and keep vacancy short during PCS season.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Columbus, GA | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Columbus, GA single-family rental renovation: tenant-ready scopes for ranches near Fort Benning, mill houses and Midtown homes, with fast turns.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovations in Columbus, Georgia
rental-renovation.intro:
Columbus has a deep single-family rental market, driven by Fort Benning, the hospitals, Columbus State University and a large local workforce. Rental owners here range from service members who kept their house after a transfer to investors and funds holding dozens of ranches across south and east Columbus and Phenix City.

Genstone Construction scopes Columbus rental renovations around durability, tenant comfort and predictable maintenance. Before you buy, a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review puts a number on the work; after you buy, the detailed scope lists labor, materials and the draw schedule. Portfolio owners can set common specifications across houses, and a designated field manager coordinates licensed local contractors and documents the work. Genstone Field Services is available for turns, inspections and occupied maintenance between renovation projects.

sections.h2: A rental standard for Columbus ranches
sections.body:
The brick ranches that fill much of south and east Columbus share familiar needs. Original single-pane or aluminum windows leak air and sweat in winter. Electrical panels may be obsolete or undersized for modern loads. Supply lines are often galvanized, and drains are often cast iron. HVAC systems may have been replaced over the years without matching ductwork. Many have enclosed carports or garages that were converted without permits.

Addressing those items during a renovation prevents many of the service calls that erode rental profits.

For owners with several properties, a consistent specification pays off. The same flooring, paint colors, cabinet style, fixtures, water heaters and HVAC equipment across every house means maintenance technicians know what to expect, parts can be stocked, and turns go faster.

We can build scopes around your existing standard or help develop one suited to the local stock. Each project is documented with photos, specifications and lien waivers, keeping records consistent across the portfolio and across both sides of the river.

sections.h2: Mill houses and older homes as Columbus rentals
sections.body:
Mill houses in Bibb City, North Highlands and Rose Hill, and older frame homes in East Wynnton and near downtown, can be inexpensive to acquire and attract tenants who want to live close to the riverfront, downtown jobs or Columbus State University's RiverPark campus.

They also need more work. Piers have often settled, especially on slopes. Termites and rot often reach the sills and floor joists. Wiring may include knob-and-tube. Plumbing is frequently a mix of old and new materials, and roofs may be near the end of their life.

We recommend addressing structure, termite damage, wiring, plumbing and roofing before spending on finishes. Crawlspace vapor barriers and drainage corrections reduce moisture problems over the long term.

Original heart pine floors in mill houses are often worth refinishing and hold up well under tenants. Painted wood trim can usually be restored.

If the house sits in a historic district, exterior work may need review, which affects windows and siding choices. We check designation early.

sections.h2: Turns, inspections and upkeep in Columbus
sections.body:
Military rotations mean many Columbus rentals turn over on a predictable rhythm, often with a burst of moves in the warmer months. A fast turn is the difference between a short gap and a lost month.

Genstone Field Services handles make-ready work, cleaning, paint touch-ups, small repairs and inspections. When a turn uncovers bigger needs, such as a failing HVAC system, roof leak, termite activity or water heater at the end of its life, our renovation team scopes and prices the repair so you can decide quickly.

Move-out conditions are documented with photos, giving owners and property managers a clear basis for separating tenant damage from normal wear.

Occupied maintenance helps too. Servicing HVAC before summer, cleaning gutters in the fall, inspecting for termites and checking roofs after spring storms catches small problems before they turn into emergencies.

For owners who have relocated with the military, documented inspections provide a clear picture of each property's condition without a trip back to Columbus.

faqs.q: Can you renovate several Columbus rentals at once?
faqs.a: Yes. Many clients acquire multiple ranches at the same time or are building portfolios across Columbus and Phenix City. Each house has a designated field manager, documented progress and a draw schedule tied to completed work. Coordinating several homes lets crews and materials move efficiently between them, and a common specification simplifies maintenance and future turns across the whole group.

faqs.q: Do you work with Columbus property managers?
faqs.a: We do. Many owners, especially those who have left the area with the military, rely on local property managers. Your manager can be our point of contact for keys, move-in dates and tenant notices, and receives the same scopes and photos you do. Genstone Property Management is also available within the Genstone Companies, though using it is not required. Owners abroad on assignment rely on this setup often.

faqs.q: Does your warranty cover tenant damage?
faqs.a: No. The one-year workmanship warranty is limited to flaws in what our contractors built or installed, so a hole punched in a door or carpet worn by a family of five is not included. We photograph conditions at completion, which makes it easier to tell later whether an issue stems from the work we performed or from use during a tenancy. That record is particularly useful in Columbus, where frequent military moves mean more move-out inspections. Photos of HVAC and flooring are the ones owners use most.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and Fourplex Renovation in Columbus, GA | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Columbus, GA duplex and 2-4 unit renovation for brick duplexes near Fort Benning, Midtown conversions and mill-area doubles, phased around tenants.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Small Multifamily Renovations in Columbus, Georgia
multifamily-renovation.intro:
Columbus has a healthy stock of small multifamily buildings, much of it tied to military and workforce housing. Brick duplexes and fourplexes from the 1950s through the 1970s sit in neighborhoods near Fort Benning and along major corridors in south and east Columbus. Older houses in Midtown and near downtown have been divided into apartments. Frame doubles appear in the mill neighborhoods along the river.

Genstone Construction scopes two- to four-unit Columbus properties with attention to shared systems, unit separation and occupied-unit phasing. Big-ticket items such as roofs, sewer lines and electrical service show up in the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, before you are committed. A detailed scope and draw schedule follow, and a designated field manager coordinates licensed local contractors, permits and inspections through the consolidated government.

sections.h2: Brick duplexes and fourplexes near Fort Benning
sections.body:
The purpose-built duplexes and fourplexes in south and east Columbus are among the most straightforward small multifamily properties to renovate. Their masonry exteriors hold up well, layouts are simple, and units are usually separated by masonry or framed walls.

Their needs are predictable. Original windows, aging roofs, outdated electrical panels, galvanized supply lines, cast-iron drains and HVAC systems at the end of their life are common. Kitchens and baths are often original or have been updated cheaply over the years.

In fourplexes, shared components deserve close attention. The roof, sewer lateral, water service and any shared laundry or utility room serve every unit, and a failure affects all tenants. Separate meters and individual HVAC systems and water heaters, where not already in place, reduce disputes and let each unit operate independently.

For military tenants, durable finishes matter. Luxury vinyl plank, scrubbable paint and simple fixtures hold up through frequent moves. Laundry hookups in each unit, where space allows, can improve rentability.

Older houses in Midtown and near downtown that were divided into apartments decades ago vary widely in quality. Some conversions were properly permitted with fire separation and individual utilities. Others share meters and heating, rely on improvised stairs or exits, or were never permitted at all.

Before buying, it is important to confirm the legal unit count with the consolidated government. If the current use is not legal, the renovation plan and the value of the building change significantly.

Frame doubles in North Highlands, Bibb City and Rose Hill share the issues of single mill houses: settled piers, termite damage, outdated wiring and mixed plumbing. Because the two units share a roof, foundation and party wall, a problem on one side often affects the other.

We scope these buildings as one structure for foundation, roof and exterior, and as separate units for interiors and systems. In these doubles, the shared wall often has little or no fire-rated construction, and correcting that is a priority. In historic districts, exterior changes may require review before permits issue.

sections.h2: Keeping Columbus tenants in place during work
sections.body:
Many small multifamily properties in Columbus change hands with tenants still living there. Renovating around them requires planning.

Occupied units keep water, power, cooling and safe access throughout the project. When shared systems must be shut down, such as during a water service replacement, sewer repair or electrical upgrade, we schedule the work and notify tenants in advance through you or your property manager.

Vacant units are renovated first where possible. Tenants can then move into finished units while their original apartments are updated, which keeps rent flowing.

In occupied buildings, daily cleanup, dust control, secure material storage and reasonable work hours make a real difference to tenant relations. Many military households have young children, so site safety and clear communication about work areas are especially important.

Our field manager tracks progress unit by unit and ties every draw to finished work. Lien waivers and inspection records are collected throughout, which supports refinancing or selling the building afterward.

faqs.q: How do I confirm a Columbus conversion is legal?
faqs.a: Check zoning and permit history with the Columbus Consolidated Government before buying. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, our team also looks for signs of unpermitted conversion work, such as shared meters, missing fire separation or improvised exits. If the legal unit count is lower than the current use, the renovation plan and the building's value change significantly, so it is worth confirming early.

faqs.q: Should each unit in a Columbus fourplex have its own HVAC and water heater?
faqs.a: In most cases it makes sense. Individual systems let tenants control their own comfort and utility costs, and a single failure affects only one unit. The cost depends on the building's existing layout and utility service. We price separation in the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can weigh the upfront cost against long-term savings and easier management of the building.

faqs.q: Can you renovate while my tenants live in the building?
faqs.a: Yes. We phase the work so occupied units keep essential services, schedule shared-system shutdowns with notice and keep work areas clean and secure. Our field manager communicates with you or your property manager so tenants know what is coming. Where possible, we renovate vacant units first so tenants can move into finished space and the rent keeps coming in. Military households with children get advance notice of noisy work days.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Columbus, GA | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor for Columbus, GA buyers, agents and lenders: bids for Midtown bungalows and base-area ranches, plus draw paperwork.
fha-203k.intro:
In Columbus, the FHA 203(k) program often helps buyers who would otherwise be stuck between a move-in-ready house they cannot afford and a fixer-upper they cannot finance. Midtown bungalows with outdated kitchens and wiring, ranches near Fort Benning with tired systems, and older homes in the mill neighborhoods can all become workable purchases when the renovation is rolled into the mortgage.

Genstone Construction carries FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status and works with buyers, real estate agents and lenders across the Columbus area. Our role covers the itemized bid, coordination with the HUD consultant when the loan is Standard, and construction through each lender draw. One field manager stays with the house from bid to final, and the permit, review, inspection and lien waiver work stays on our side of the table.

sections.h2: Matching the 203(k) version to a Columbus house
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) is meant for non-structural work and is capped at $75,000 in repairs. Brick ranches in south and east Columbus often fit well: a new kitchen, updated baths, flooring, roof, windows, HVAC or a water heater, with no structural work required.

Structural or larger projects go under the Standard 203(k), which starts at a $5,000 minimum in repairs and brings a HUD-approved consultant into the process. Midtown homes needing layout changes or additions, Historic District houses with pier and framing problems, and mill houses that need releveling and termite repair usually fall here.

A useful rule of thumb in Columbus: if the floors slope noticeably, the porch is pulling away, or the plan involves moving walls or adding square footage, expect the Standard program. If the house is structurally sound and the work is cosmetic and mechanical, the Limited program may be enough.

We help buyers and agents sort this out before the loan application, which avoids delays caused by switching programs later.

sections.h2: Columbus homes that make sense for 203(k)
sections.body:
The strongest 203(k) candidates in Columbus combine a fair price with a sound structure.

Post-war brick ranches near Fort Benning and in east Columbus are frequent choices. Their masonry exteriors mean renovation dollars go toward kitchens, baths and systems that buyers use every day. Many military families who plan to stay in the area after service, or civilian employees at the base, find these homes a practical path to ownership.

Midtown bungalows and revival-style homes attract buyers who want older homes in established neighborhoods. Under the Standard program, they can be updated thoughtfully, though wiring, plumbing and crawlspace work may take a larger share of the budget than expected.

Mill houses are the most challenging. Low purchase prices are appealing, but foundation, framing and termite work can be extensive.

For homes built before 1978, lead-safe work practices apply when painted surfaces are disturbed, and that must be in the bid. Exterior work in historic districts requires review. We raise these points early.

A 203(k) renovation carries more paperwork than a typical project. Our bids break out labor and materials by trade and room, organized the way lenders and consultants review them.

On Standard loans, the consultant's work write-up defines the scope, and we coordinate with them to align our bid before closing. Any differences are resolved before the loan funds, so there are no surprises once work begins.

During construction, the lender releases money in draws as work is completed and verified. Each request is supported by photos, inspection and lien waivers. For Limited loans, repair amounts above $15,000 trigger additional inspection requirements.

Permits for properties in Columbus come through the consolidated government's inspections office, and work in the Historic District or other local districts goes before the Board of Historic and Architectural Review first. Homes in Harris County or across the river in Alabama follow their own processes.

We keep the buyer and agent informed throughout, so everyone knows what is complete and what comes next.

faqs.q: Can military buyers use a 203(k) loan in Columbus?
faqs.a: Yes, if they qualify for FHA financing and plan to occupy the home. Many military families use VA loans instead, and the VA has its own renovation loan options with different rules. We work with buyers and lenders on FHA 203(k) projects and can provide bids in the format either program requires. The buyer's lender is the right source for comparing the options.

faqs.q: Do Columbus agents bring you into 203(k) deals?
faqs.a: Yes. Agents often contact us while their buyer is considering a property. We walk the house, explain which program fits and provide an itemized bid for the loan file. That helps agents set realistic expectations about timing and paperwork, and it can help a buyer decide whether a specific house is the right fit before making an offer on it.

faqs.q: What happens if you find hidden damage during a Columbus 203(k)?
faqs.a: Older Columbus homes can reveal termite damage, rotted sills or wiring problems once work begins. The program includes a contingency reserve for unforeseen repairs. We document the condition with photos, price the repair and submit a change order through the lender, so additional work is approved before it proceeds and the project remains in compliance. In Columbus mill houses, the sills and floor framing under bathrooms are where that kind of discovery happens most often, so we look closely there before the bid is finalized.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Columbus, GA | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Columbus, GA REO and bank-owned renovation for servicers and GSEs: vacant ranch and mill house repairs, code compliance and documented draws.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Renovations in Columbus, Georgia
reo-renovation.intro:
Bank-owned homes in Columbus often come from the same rental-heavy neighborhoods that serve Fort Benning, along with older mill houses and Midtown properties that slipped into foreclosure. Vacancy in this climate brings mold, termite damage, roof leaks and overgrown lots, and servicers, banks, funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises need those homes stabilized, repaired and documented before they can be sold.

Genstone Construction is on the preferred contractor list for GSEs, and its leadership has spent decades on REO, flip and remodeling work for servicers, banks and asset managers. In Columbus and the surrounding area, including Phenix City, we scope vacant homes for local conditions, coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors and document every step. Genstone Field Services supports the renovation with preservation, inspections and code compliance work.

sections.body:
A Columbus house left empty through a summer can change quickly. With the power or air conditioning off, humidity builds, and mold appears on drywall, cabinets and closet walls. A roof leak that would have been caught by an occupant goes unnoticed until a ceiling sags.

Termites are active through much of the year, and vacant homes without regular treatment can lose sills, joists and porch framing.

In the ranch neighborhoods, vacancy also invites theft. Copper, HVAC condensers and appliances are frequent targets. Broken windows and forced doors lead to further damage.

Older mill houses face added risks. Their light framing, older roofs and settled piers deteriorate faster when no one is maintaining gutters or reporting leaks.

Winter freezes are uncommon but can still split pipes in vacant homes with the heat off.

We begin every REO project with a documented condition assessment. Immediate stabilization, including securing openings, stopping leaks and drying out the house, is separated from the renovation scope, so asset managers see costs and priorities clearly.

sections.h2: Columbus code compliance, permits and records
sections.body:
Vacant homes in Columbus can draw code enforcement attention for overgrown yards, open structures, damaged roofs and debris. Violations left unresolved can lead to fines or liens that complicate a sale.

Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, inspections and code compliance, including lawn care, securing openings, debris removal and documentation of each resolved violation.

On the renovation side, permits for structural, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work are pulled through the Columbus Consolidated Government or the appropriate jurisdiction in Harris County or Alabama. Historic district properties may need review before exterior work begins.

We look for open permits left by prior owners, since they can hold up a closing, and we flag unpermitted conversions that may affect how the property is marketed. Genstone's Title Clearing & Escrow company can help where title problems arise.

Draw packages carry photos and lien waivers for each phase, which is the paper trail servicer and GSE reviewers look for.

Columbus has a large pool of buyers using VA and FHA financing, and that shapes many REO decisions. Those loans require homes to meet minimum property standards: working mechanical systems, a roof without active leaks, intact paint on pre-1978 surfaces and no obvious safety hazards. Making those repairs can widen the buyer pool considerably, especially for ranches near Fort Benning.

Investor buyers, on the other hand, often prefer a lower price and their own finishes. For homes likely to sell to investors, a lighter scope focused on safety, securing, mold remediation and termite treatment may be the better choice.

Asset managers get a light, a middle and, where it makes sense, a full scope priced together. In Midtown and north Columbus, where renovated comps are stronger, a fuller renovation may be justified. In mill neighborhoods and some parts of south Columbus, a lighter approach is often more efficient.

Whatever the scope, our field manager documents the work from intake to completion, and draws are released only for finished, verified work.

faqs.q: Do you handle REO properties in Phenix City?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate licensed local contractors in Phenix City and Russell County, Alabama, as well as Columbus and Harris County, Georgia. Each side of the river has its own permitting and licensing rules, and our team handles permits accordingly. Reporting, draws and documentation follow the same standards on both sides, which keeps files consistent for servicers with properties in both states.

faqs.q: Can you prepare Columbus REO homes for VA buyers?
faqs.a: We can scope repairs aimed at meeting VA minimum property requirements, such as working HVAC and plumbing, a sound roof, safe electrical and no deteriorated paint on older homes. Final approval depends on the appraiser and lender, but addressing these items up front reduces the chance of repair conditions delaying a sale, which matters in a market with so many military buyers.

faqs.q: How do you report on Columbus REO projects?
faqs.a: Each project has a designated field manager who photographs the property at intake, at milestones and at completion. Draw requests are backed by that documentation, and lien waivers and permit records are collected throughout. Asset managers can review status remotely and keep their files complete without sending anyone to Columbus to check on the work in person. We can also match your preferred report format and photo naming.
